Visual Basic.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that property names match a provided regular expression.

Visual Basic.Title: Non-private constants should comply with a naming convention
Visual Basic.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private Const field names comply with the provided regular expression.

C#.Title: Public methods should not have multidimensional array parameters
C#.Description: Using multidimensional and jagged arrays as method parameters in C# can be challenging for developers.

Visual Basic.Title: Public methods should not have multidimensional array parameters
Visual Basic.Description: Using multidimensional and jagged arrays as method parameters in C# can be challenging for developers.

Visual Basic.Title: Non-private fields should comply with a naming convention
Visual Basic.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private fields names match a provided regular expression.

Visual Basic.Title: Non-private "Shared ReadOnly" fields should comply with a naming convention
Visual Basic.Description: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private Shared ReadOnly fields names match a provided regular expression.

C#.Title: Exceptions should not be thrown from property getters
C#.Description: Property getters should be simple operations that are always safe to call. If exceptions need to be thrown, it is best to convert the property to a method.

Visual Basic.Title: Exceptions should not be thrown from property getters
Visual Basic.Description: Property getters should be simple operations that are always safe to call. If exceptions need to be thrown, it is best to convert the property to a method.

Visual Basic.Title: Generic type parameter names should comply with a naming convention
Visual Basic.Description: This rule is deprecated; use {rule:vbnet:S119} instead.

Visual Basic.Title: Signed types should be preferred to unsigned ones
Visual Basic.Description: Unsigned integers have different arithmetic operators than signed ones - operators that few developers understand. Therefore, signed types should be preferred where possible.

Visual Basic.Title: "With" statements should be used for a series of calls to the same object
Visual Basic.Description: Using the With statement for a series of calls to the same object makes the code more readable.

C#.Title: Write-only properties should not be used
C#.Description: Properties with only setters are confusing and counterintuitive. Instead, a property getter should be added if possible, or the property should be replaced with a setter method.

Visual Basic.Title: Write-only properties should not be used
Visual Basic.Description: Properties with only setters are confusing and counterintuitive. Instead, a property getter should be added if possible, or the property should be replaced with a setter method.

C#.Title: Mutable fields should not be "public static"
C#.Description: public static mutable fields of classes which are accessed directly should be protected to the degree possible. This can be done by reducing the accessibility of the field or by changing the return type to an immutable type.

C#.Title: Child class fields should not shadow parent class fields
C#.Description: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

Visual Basic.Title: Child class fields should not shadow parent class fields
Visual Basic.Description: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

Visual Basic.Title: Arrays should be initialized using the "... = {}" syntax
Visual Basic.Description: The ... = {} syntax is more compact, more readable and less error-prone.

C#.Title: Types and methods should not have too many generic parameters
C#.Description: A method or class with too many type parameters has likely aggregated too many responsibilities and should be split.

C#.Title: Unnecessary bit operations should not be performed
C#.Description: Certain bitwise operations are not needed and should not be performed because their results are predictable.

Visual Basic.Title: Unnecessary bit operations should not be performed
Visual Basic.Description: Certain bitwise operations are not needed and should not be performed because their results are predictable.

C#.Title: Blocks should be synchronized on read-only fields
C#.Description: Locking on a class field synchronizes not on the field itself, but on the object assigned to it. Thus, there are some good practices to follow to avoid problems related to thread synchronization.

C#.Title: Whitespace and control characters in string literals should be explicit
C#.Description: Non-encoded control characters and whitespace characters are often injected in the source code because of a bad manipulation. They are either invisible or difficult to recognize, which can result in bugs when the string is not what the developer expects. If you actually need to use a control character use their encoded version:

C#.Title: Generic exceptions should not be ignored
C#.Description: When exceptions occur, it is usually a bad idea to simply ignore them. Instead, it is better to handle them properly, or at least to log them.

C#.Title: Shared resources should not be used for locking
C#.Description: The instance passed to the lock statement should be a dedicated private field.

Visual Basic.Title: Shared resources should not be used for locking
Visual Basic.Description: The instance passed to the SyncLock statement should be a dedicated private field.

C#.Title: Setting loose file permissions is security-sensitive
C#.Description: In Unix, "others" class refers to all users except the owner of the file and the members of the group assigned to this file.

Visual Basic.Title: Setting loose POSIX file permissions is security-sensitive
Visual Basic.Description: In Unix, "others" class refers to all users except the owner of the file and the members of the group assigned to this file.

C#.Title: Logging templates should be constant
C#.Description: Logging arguments should not require evaluation in order to avoid unnecessary performance overhead. When passing concatenated strings or string interpolations directly into a logging method, the evaluation of these expressions occurs every time the logging method is called, regardless of the log level. This can lead to inefficient code execution and increased resource consumption.

C#.Title: The length returned from a stream read should be checked
C#.Description: Invoking a stream reading method without verifying the number of bytes read can lead to erroneous assumptions. A Stream can represent any I/O operation, such as reading a file, network communication, or inter-process communication. As such, it is not guaranteed that the byte[] passed into the method will be filled with the requested number of bytes. Therefore, inspecting the value returned by the reading method is important to ensure the number of bytes read.

C#.Title: Multiline blocks should be enclosed in curly braces
C#.Description: Having inconsistent indentation and omitting curly braces from a control structure, such as an if statement or for loop, is misleading and can induce bugs.

C#.Title: "NaN" should not be used in comparisons
C#.Description: double.NaN and float.NaN are not equal to anything, not even themselves.

C#.Title: "IndexOf" checks should not be for positive numbers
C#.Description: Most checks against an IndexOf value compare it with -1 because 0 is a valid index.

Visual Basic.Title: "IndexOf" checks should not be for positive numbers
Visual Basic.Description: Most checks against an IndexOf value compare it with -1 because 0 is a valid index.

C#.Title: Instance members should not write to "static" fields
C#.Description: This rule raises an issue each time a static field is updated from a non-static method or property.

C#.Title: Tests should include assertions
C#.Description: The rule targets test methods that lack an assertion and consist solely of an action and, optionally, a setup.

C#.Title: Literal boolean values should not be used in assertions
C#.Description: Using literal boolean values in assertions can lead to less readable and less informative unit tests. When a test fails, it’s important to have a clear understanding of what the test was checking and why it failed. Most of the testing frameworks provide more explicit assertion methods that will provide a more helpful error message if the test fails.

C#.Title: "catch" clauses should do more than rethrow
C#.Description: A catch clause that only rethrows the caught exception has the same effect as omitting the catch altogether and letting it bubble up automatically.

Visual Basic.Title: "catch" clauses should do more than rethrow
Visual Basic.Description: A Catch clause that only rethrows the caught exception has the same effect as omitting the Catch altogether and letting it bubble up automatically.

C#.Title: Static fields should not be used in generic types
C#.Description: A static field in a generic type is not shared among instances of different closed constructed types, thus LengthLimitedSingletonCollection<int>.instances and LengthLimitedSingletonCollection<string>.instances will point to different objects, even though instances is seemingly shared among all LengthLimitedSingletonCollection<> generic classes.

C#.Title: XML parsers should not be vulnerable to XXE attacks
C#.Description: This vulnerability allows the usage of external entities in XML.

C#.Title: Non-existent operators like "=+" should not be used
C#.Description: Using operator pairs (=+, =-, or =!) that look like reversed single operators (+=, -= or !=) is confusing. They compile and run but do not produce the same result as their mirrored counterpart.

Visual Basic.Title: Non-existent operators like "=+" should not be used
Visual Basic.Description: Using operator pairs (=+ or =-) that look like reversed single operators (+= or -=) is confusing. They compile and run but do not produce the same result as their mirrored counterpart.

C#.Title: Sequential tests should not check the same condition
C#.Description: When the same condition is checked twice in a row, it is either confusing - why have separate checks? - or an error - some other condition should have been checked in the second test.

C#.Title: Doubled prefix operators "!!" and "~~" should not be used
C#.Description: The repetition of a prefix operator (!, or ~) is usually a typo. The second operator invalidates the first one.

Visual Basic.Title: 'Not' boolean operator should not be repeated
Visual Basic.Description: The repetition of the Not operator is usually a typo. The second operator invalidates the first one:

C#.Title: SQL keywords should be delimited by whitespace
C#.Description: When concatenating strings, it is very easy to forget a whitespace.

C#.Title: "Thread.Sleep" should not be used in tests
C#.Description: Using Thread.Sleep in a test might introduce unpredictable and inconsistent results depending on the environment. Furthermore, it will block the thread, which means the system resources are not being fully used.

Visual Basic.Title: "Thread.Sleep" should not be used in tests
Visual Basic.Description: Using Thread.Sleep in a test might introduce unpredictable and inconsistent results depending on the environment. Furthermore, it will block the thread, which means the system resources are not being fully used.

C#.Title: "IDisposables" should be disposed
C#.Description: When writing managed code, there is no need to worry about memory allocation or deallocation as it is taken care of by the garbage collector. However, certain objects, such as Bitmap, utilize unmanaged memory for specific purposes like pointer arithmetic. These objects may have substantial unmanaged memory footprints while having minimal managed footprints. Unfortunately, the garbage collector only recognizes the small managed footprint and does not promptly reclaim the corresponding unmanaged memory (by invoking the finalizer method of Bitmap) for efficiency reasons.

C#.Title: Classes with "IDisposable" members should implement "IDisposable"
C#.Description: An IDisposable object should be disposed (there are some rare exceptions where not disposing is fine, most notably Task). If a class has an IDisposable field, there can be two situations:

C#.Title: Fields that are only assigned in the constructor should be "readonly"
C#.Description: readonly fields can only be assigned in a class constructor. If a class has a field that’s not marked readonly but is only set in the constructor, it could cause confusion about the field’s intended use. To avoid confusion, such fields should be marked readonly to make their intended use explicit, and to prevent future maintainers from inadvertently changing their use.

C#.Title: Property assignments should not be made for "readonly" fields not constrained to reference types
C#.Description: While the properties of a readonly reference type field can still be changed after initialization, those of a readonly value type field, such as a struct, cannot.

Visual Basic.Title: "Exit Select" statements should not be used redundantly
Visual Basic.Description: Visual Basic .NET, unlike many other programming languages, has no "fall-through" for its Select cases. Each case already has an implicit Exit Select as its last instruction. It therefore is redundant to explicitly add one.

C#.Title: Classes should "Dispose" of members from the classes' own "Dispose" methods
C#.Description: It is possible in an IDisposable to call Dispose on class members from any method, but the contract of Dispose is that it will clean up all unmanaged resources. Move disposing of members to some other method, and you risk resource leaks.

C#.Title: Methods named "Dispose" should implement "IDisposable.Dispose"
C#.Description: IDisposable is an interface implemented by all types which need to provide a mechanism for releasing unmanaged resources.

C#.Title: Generic parameters not constrained to reference types should not be compared to "null"
C#.Description: In C#, without constraints on a generic type parameter, both reference and value types can be passed. However, comparing this type parameter to null can be misleading as value types, like struct, can never be null.

C#.Title: Assertions should be complete
C#.Description: This rule addresses the issue of incomplete assertions that can occur when using certain test frameworks. Incomplete assertions can lead to tests that do not effectively verify anything. The rule enforces the use of complete assertions in specific cases, namely:

C#.Title: LINQ expressions should be simplified
C#.Description: In the interests of readability, code that can be simplified should be simplified. To that end, there are several ways IEnumerable language integrated queries (LINQ) can be simplified. This not only improves readabilty but can also lead to improved performance.

C#.Title: "Object.ReferenceEquals" should not be used for value types
C#.Description: In C#, the Object.ReferenceEquals method is used to compare two reference type variables. If you use this method to compare two value types, such as int, float, or bool you will not get the expected results because value type variables contain an instance of the type and not a reference to it.

C#.Title: "ThreadStatic" fields should not be initialized
C#.Description: When an object has a field annotated with ThreadStatic, that field is shared within a given thread, but unique across threads. Since a class' static initializer is only invoked for the first thread created, it also means that only the first thread will have the expected initial values.

C#.Title: "IDisposables" created in a "using" statement should not be returned
C#.Description: When you use a using statement, the goal is to ensure the correct disposal of an IDisposable instance when the control leaves the using statement block.

C#.Title: "ThreadStatic" should not be used on non-static fields
C#.Description: When you annotate a field with the ThreadStatic attribute, it is an indication that the value of this field is unique for each thread. But if you don’t mark the field as static, then the ThreadStatic attribute is ignored.

C#.Title: Static fields should not be updated in constructors
C#.Description: Assigning a value to a static field in a constructor could cause unreliable behavior at runtime since it will change the value for all instances of the class.

C#.Title: Reflection should not be used to increase accessibility of classes, methods, or fields
C#.Description: Altering or bypassing the accessibility of classes, methods, or fields through reflection violates the encapsulation principle. This can break the internal contracts of the accessed target and lead to maintainability issues and runtime errors.

Visual Basic.Title: Reflection should not be used to increase accessibility of classes, methods, or fields
Visual Basic.Description: Altering or bypassing the accessibility of classes, methods, or fields through reflection violates the encapsulation principle. This can break the internal contracts of the accessed target and lead to maintainability issues and runtime errors.

C#.Title: Members should not be initialized to default values
C#.Description: The compiler automatically initializes class fields, auto-properties and events to their default values before setting them with any initialization values, so there is no need to explicitly set a member to its default value. Further, under the logic that cleaner code is better code, it’s considered poor style to do so.

C#.Title: Types should not have members with visibility set higher than the type's visibility
C#.Description: There’s no point in having a public member in a non-public type because objects that can’t access the type will never have the chance to access the member.

C#.Title: "is" should not be used with "this"
C#.Description: One of the possible ways of performing type-testing is via the is operator: food is Pizza.

C#.Title: "StringBuilder" data should be used
C#.Description: StringBuilder instances that never build a string clutter the code and worse are a drag on performance. Either they should be removed, or the missing ToString() call should be added.

Visual Basic.Title: "StringBuilder" data should be used
Visual Basic.Description: StringBuilder instances that never build a string clutter the code and worse are a drag on performance. Either they should be removed, or the missing ToString() call should be added.

C#.Title: "async" methods should not return "void"
C#.Description: An async method with a void return type does not follow the task asynchronous programming (TAP) model since the return type should be Task or Task<TResult>

C#.Title: Multiple "OrderBy" calls should not be used
C#.Description: There’s no point in chaining multiple OrderBy calls in a LINQ; only the last one will be reflected in the result because each subsequent call completely reorders the list. Thus, calling OrderBy multiple times is a performance issue as well, because all of the sorting will be executed, but only the result of the last sort will be kept.

C#.Title: Delegates should not be subtracted
C#.Description: In C#, delegates can be added together to chain their execution, and subtracted to remove their execution from the chain.

C#.Title: "interface" instances should not be cast to concrete types
C#.Description: Needing to cast from an interface to a concrete type indicates that something is wrong with the abstractions in use, likely that something is missing from the interface. Instead of casting to a discrete type, the missing functionality should be added to the interface. Otherwise there is a risk of runtime exceptions.

C#.Title: "ConfigureAwait(false)" should be used
C#.Description: After an awaited Task has executed, you can continue execution in the original, calling thread or any arbitrary thread. Unless the rest of the code needs the context from which the Task was spawned, Task.ConfigureAwait(false) should be used to keep execution in the Task thread to avoid the need for context switching and the possibility of deadlocks.

C#.Title: "Explicit" conversions of "foreach" loops should not be used
C#.Description: The foreach statement was introduced in the C# language prior to generics to make it easier to work with the non-generic collections available at that time such as ArrayList. The foreach statements allow you to downcast elements of a collection of Objects to any other type.

C#.Title: Inner class members should not shadow outer class "static" or type members
C#.Description: Naming the members of an inner class the same as the static members of its enclosing class is possible but generally considered a bad practice. That’s because maintainers may be confused about which members are being used in a given context. Instead the inner class member should be given distinct and descriptive name, and all references to it should be updated accordingly.

C#.Title: Method calls should not resolve ambiguously to overloads with "params"
C#.Description: The rules for method resolution are complex and perhaps not properly understood by all coders. The params keyword can make method declarations overlap in non-obvious ways, so that slight changes in the argument types of an invocation can resolve to different methods.

C#.Title: "GC.SuppressFinalize" should not be invoked for types without destructors
C#.Description: GC.SuppressFinalize asks the Common Language Runtime not to call the finalizer of an object. This is useful when implementing the dispose pattern where object finalization is already handled in IDisposable.Dispose. However, it has no effect if there is no finalizer defined in the object’s type, so using it in such cases is just confusing.

C#.Title: Redundant parentheses should not be used
C#.Description: Redundant parentheses are simply wasted keystrokes, and should be removed.

C#.Title: Caller information arguments should not be provided explicitly
C#.Description: Caller information attributes: CallerFilePathAttribute, CallerLineNumberAttribute, and CallerArgumentExpressionAttribute provide a way to get information about the caller of a method through optional parameters. But the arguments for these optional parameters are only generated if they are not explicitly defined in the call. Thus, specifying the argument values defeats the purpose of the attributes.

C#.Title: "value" contextual keyword should be used
C#.Description: When you need to get external input for set and init methods defined for properties and indexers or for remove and add methods for events, you should always get this input throught the value contextual keyword.

C#.Title: The simplest possible condition syntax should be used
C#.Description: In the interests of keeping code clean, the simplest possible conditional syntax should be used. That means

C#.Title: Methods should not return values that are never used
C#.Description: Private methods are intended for use only within their scope. If these methods return values that are not utilized by any calling functions, it indicates that the return operation is unnecessary. Removing such returns can enhance both efficiency and code clarity.

C#.Title: Method parameters should be declared with base types
C#.Description: When a derived type is used as a parameter instead of the base type, it limits the uses of the method. If the additional functionality that is provided in the derived type is not required then that limitation isn’t required, and should be removed.

C#.Title: Anonymous delegates should not be used to unsubscribe from Events
C#.Description: When working with anonymous functions, it is important to keep in mind that each time you create one, it is a completely new instance.

C#.Title: Generic type parameters should be co/contravariant when possible
C#.Description: In the interests of making code as usable as possible, interfaces and delegates with generic parameters should use the out and in modifiers when possible to make the interfaces and delegates covariant and contravariant, respectively.

C#.Title: Duplicate casts should not be made
C#.Description: In C#, the is type testing operator can be used to check if the run-time type of an object is compatible with a given type. If the object is not null, then the is operator performs a cast, and so performing another cast following the check result is redundant.

C#.Title: Classes directly extending "object" should not call "base" in "GetHashCode" or "Equals"
C#.Description: Making a base call when overriding a method is generally a good idea, but not in the case of GetHashCode and Equals for classes that directly extend Object. These methods are based on the object’s reference, meaning that no two objects that use those base methods can be equal or have the same hash.

C#.Title: Implementations should be provided for "partial" methods
C#.Description: partial methods allow an increased degree of flexibility in programming a system. Hooks can be added to generated code by invoking methods that define their signature, but might not have an implementation yet. But if the implementation is still missing when the code makes it to production, the compiler silently removes the call. In the best case scenario, such calls simply represent cruft, but in they worst case they are critical, missing functionality, the loss of which will lead to unexpected results at runtime.

C#.Title: Constructor and destructor declarations should not be redundant
C#.Description: Since the compiler will automatically invoke the base type’s no-argument constructor, there’s no need to specify its invocation explicitly. Also, when only a single public parameterless constructor is defined in a class, then that constructor can be removed because the compiler would generate it automatically. Similarly, empty static constructors and empty destructors are also wasted keystrokes.

C#.Title: Default parameter values should not be passed as arguments
C#.Description: Specifying the default parameter values in a method call is redundant. Such values should be omitted in the interests of readability.

C#.Title: "string.IsNullOrEmpty" should be used
C#.Description: Using string.Equals to determine if a string is empty is significantly slower than using string.IsNullOrEmpty() or checking for string.Length == 0. string.IsNullOrEmpty() is both clear and concise, and therefore preferred to laborious, error-prone, manual null- and emptiness-checking.

C#.Title: Declarations and initializations should be as concise as possible
C#.Description: In C#, the type of a variable can often be inferred by the compiler. The use of the [var keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/implicitly-typed-local-variables) allows you to avoid repeating the type name in a variable declaration and object instantiation because the declared type can often be inferred by the compiler.

C#.Title: Non-derived "private" classes and records should be "sealed"
C#.Description: Classes and records with either private or file access modifiers aren’t visible outside of their assemblies or files, so if they’re not extended inside their scope, they should be made explicitly non-extensible with the addition of the sealed keyword.

C#.Title: Namespaces should not be empty
C#.Description: Namespaces with no lines of code clutter a project and should be removed.

C#.Title: "params" should be used on overrides
C#.Description: Overriding methods automatically inherit the params behavior. To ease readability, this modifier should be explicitly used in the overriding method as well.

C#.Title: Static fields should appear in the order they must be initialized
C#.Description: Static field initializers are executed in the order in which they appear in the class from top to bottom. Thus, placing a static field in a class above the field or fields required for its initialization will yield unexpected results.

C#.Title: Events should be invoked
C#.Description: Events that are not invoked anywhere are dead code, and there’s no good reason to keep them in the source.

C#.Title: Non-flags enums should not be used in bitwise operations
C#.Description: Enumerations are commonly used to identify distinct elements from a set of values.

C#.Title: Loops should be simplified with "LINQ" expressions
C#.Description: Using explicit loops for filtering, selecting, or aggregating elements can make code more verbose and harder to read. LINQ expressions provide a more concise and expressive way to perform these operations, improving code clarity and maintainability.

C#.Title: Creating cookies without the "HttpOnly" flag is security-sensitive
C#.Description: When a cookie is configured with the HttpOnly attribute set to true, the browser guaranties that no client-side script will be able to read it. In most cases, when a cookie is created, the default value of HttpOnly is false and it’s up to the developer to decide whether or not the content of the cookie can be read by the client-side script. As a majority of Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks target the theft of session-cookies, the HttpOnly attribute can help to reduce their impact as it won’t be possible to exploit the XSS vulnerability to steal session-cookies.

C#.Title: Caller information parameters should come at the end of the parameter list
C#.Description: Caller information attributes provide a way to get information about the caller of a method through optional parameters. But they only work right if their values aren’t provided explicitly. So if you define a method with caller info attributes in the middle of the parameter list, the caller is forced to use named arguments if they want to use the method properly.

C#.Title: Expressions used in "Debug.Assert" should not produce side effects
C#.Description: An assertion is a piece of code that’s used during development when the compilation debug mode is activated. It allows a program to check itself as it runs. When an assertion is true, that means everything is operating as expected.

C#.Title: Unchanged variables should be marked as "const"
C#.Description: If a variable that is not supposed to change is not marked as const, it could be accidentally reassigned elsewhere in the code, leading to unexpected behavior and bugs that can be hard to track down.

C#.Title: Ternary operators should not be nested
C#.Description: Nested ternaries are hard to read and can make the order of operations complex to understand.

Visual Basic.Title: If operators should not be nested
Visual Basic.Description: Nested ternaries are hard to read and can make the order of operations complex to understand.

C#.Title: Date and time should not be used as a type for primary keys
C#.Description: You should only set a property of a temporal type (like DateTime or DateTimeOffset) as the primary key of a table if the values are guaranteed to be unique.

Visual Basic.Title: Date and time should not be used as a type for primary keys
Visual Basic.Description: You should only set a property of a temporal type (like DateTime or DateTimeOffset) as the primary key of a table if the values are guaranteed to be unique.

C#.Title: "this" should not be exposed from constructors
C#.Description: In single-threaded environments, the use of this in constructors is normal, and expected. But in multi-threaded environments, it could expose partially-constructed objects to other threads, and should be used with caution.

C#.Title: Attribute, EventArgs, and Exception type names should end with the type being extended
C#.Description: Adherence to the standard naming conventions makes your code not only more readable, but more usable. For instance, class FirstAttribute : Attribute can be used simply with First, but you must use the full name for class AttributeOne : Attribute.

Visual Basic.Title: "Exit" statements should not be used
Visual Basic.Description: Exit Function, Exit Property, and Exit Sub are all poor, less-readable substitutes for a simple Return, and if used with code that should return a value (Exit Function and in some cases Exit Property) they could result in a NullReferenceException.

C#.Title: "base.Equals" should not be used to check for reference equality in "Equals" if "base" is not "object"
C#.Description: object.Equals() overrides can be optimized by checking first for reference equality between this and the parameter. This check can be implemented by calling object.ReferenceEquals() or base.Equals(), where base is object. However, using base.Equals() is a maintenance hazard because while it works if you extend Object directly, if you introduce a new base class that overrides Equals, it suddenly stops working.

C#.Title: "private" methods called only by inner classes should be moved to those classes
C#.Description: When a private static method is only invoked by a nested class, there’s no reason not to move it into that class. It will still have the same access to the outer class' static members, but the outer class will be clearer and less cluttered.

C#.Title: Methods should not return constants
C#.Description: There’s no point in forcing the overhead of a method call for a method that always returns the same constant value. Even worse, the fact that a method call must be made will likely mislead developers who call the method thinking that something more is done. Declare a constant instead.

C#.Title: Assertion arguments should be passed in the correct order
C#.Description: The standard assertions library methods such as AreEqual and AreSame in MSTest and NUnit, or Equal and Same in XUnit, expect the first argument to be the expected value and the second argument to be the actual value.

C#.Title: Loggers should be named for their enclosing types
C#.Description: It is a well-established convention to name each logger after its enclosing type. This rule raises an issue when the convention is not respected.

C#.Title: Method overloads with default parameter values should not overlap
C#.Description: The rules for method resolution can be complex and may not be fully understood by all developers. The situation becomes even more challenging when dealing with method overloads that have optional parameter values.

C#.Title: "[ExpectedException]" should not be used
C#.Description: It should be clear to a casual reader what code a test is testing and what results are expected. Unfortunately, that’s not usually the case with the ExpectedException attribute since an exception could be thrown from almost any line in the method.

Visual Basic.Title: "[ExpectedException]" should not be used
Visual Basic.Description: It should be clear to a casual reader what code a test is testing and what results are expected. Unfortunately, that’s not usually the case with the ExpectedException attribute since an exception could be thrown from almost any line in the method.

C#.Title: Test method signatures should be correct
C#.Description: A method is identified as a test method if it is marked with one of the following attributes:

C#.Title: Variables should not be checked against the values they're about to be assigned
C#.Description: There’s no point in checking a variable against the value you’re about to assign it. Save the cycles and lines of code, and simply perform the assignment.

C#.Title: Redundant property names should be omitted in anonymous classes
C#.Description: When an anonymous type’s properties are copied from properties or variables with the same names, it yields cleaner code to omit the new type’s property name and the assignment operator.

C#.Title: "abstract" classes should not have "public" constructors
C#.Description: The abstract modifier in a class declaration is used to indicate that a class is intended only to be a base class of other classes, not instantiated on its own.

C#.Title: Type should not be examined on "System.Type" instances
C#.Description: Calling GetType on a Type variable will always return the System.Type representation, which is equivalent to typeof(System.Type). This also applies to passing a Type argument to IsInstanceOfType which always returns false.

C#.Title: Interfaces should not simply inherit from base interfaces with colliding members
C#.Description: When an interface inherits from two interfaces that both define a member with the same name, trying to access that member through the derived interface will result in the compiler error CS0229 Ambiguity between 'IBase1.SomeProperty' and 'IBase2.SomeProperty'.

C#.Title: Exceptions should not be explicitly rethrown
C#.Description: In C#, the throw statement can be used in two different ways:

C#.Title: "[Optional]" should not be used on "ref" or "out" parameters
C#.Description: The use of ref or out in combination with Optional attribute is both confusing and contradictory. [Optional] indicates that the parameter doesn’t have to be provided, while out and ref mean that the parameter will be used to return data to the caller (ref additionally indicates that the parameter may also be used to pass data into the method).

C#.Title: Right operands of shift operators should be integers
C#.Description: Numbers can be shifted with the << and >> operators, but the right operand of the operation needs to be an int or a type that has an implicit conversion to int. However, when the left operand is dynamic, the compiler’s type checking is turned off, so you can pass anything to the right of a shift operator and have it compile. And if the argument can’t be implicitly converted to int at runtime, then a RuntimeBinderException will be raised.

Visual Basic.Title: Right operands of shift operators should be integers
Visual Basic.Description: Numbers can be shifted with the << and >> operators, but the right operand of the operation needs to be an int or a type that has an implicit conversion to int. However, when the left operand is an object, the compiler’s type checking is turned off, therfore you can pass anything to the right of a shift operator and have it compile. If the argument can’t be implicitly converted to int at runtime, a RuntimeBinderException will be raised.

C#.Title: Parameters with "[DefaultParameterValue]" attributes should also be marked "[Optional]"
C#.Description: There is no point in providing a default value for a parameter if callers are required to provide a value for it anyway. Thus, [DefaultParameterValue] should always be used in conjunction with [Optional].

C#.Title: "[DefaultValue]" should not be used when "[DefaultParameterValue]" is meant
C#.Description: DefaultValue does not make the compiler set the default value, as its name may suggest. What you probably wanted to use is DefaultParameterValue.

C#.Title: Classes should not have only "private" constructors
C#.Description: When a class has only a private constructor, it can’t be instantiated except within the class itself. Such classes can be considered dead code and should be fixed

Visual Basic.Title: Classes should not have only "private" constructors
Visual Basic.Description: When a class has only a private constructor, it can’t be instantiated except within the class itself. Such classes can be considered dead code and should be fixed

C#.Title: "string.ToCharArray()" and "ReadOnlySpan<T>.ToArray()" should not be called redundantly
C#.Description: The string type offers an indexer property that allows you to treat it as a char array. Therefore, if you just need to access a specific character or iterate over all of them, the ToCharArray call should be omitted. For these cases, not omitting makes the code harder to read and less efficient as ToCharArray copies the characters from the string object into a new Unicode character array.

C#.Title: Composite format strings should be used correctly
C#.Description: A composite format string is a string that contains placeholders, represented by indices inside curly braces "{0}", "{1}", etc. These placeholders are replaced by values when the string is printed or logged.

C#.Title: Empty "case" clauses that fall through to the "default" should be omitted
C#.Description: Empty case clauses that fall through to the default are useless. Whether or not such a case is present, the default clause will be invoked. Such cases simply clutter the code, and should be removed.

C#.Title: Unassigned members should be removed
C#.Description: Fields and auto-properties that are never assigned to hold the default values for their types. They are either pointless code or, more likely, mistakes.

C#.Title: Type inheritance should not be recursive
C#.Description: Recursion is a technique used to define a problem in terms of the problem itself, usually in terms of a simpler version of the problem itself.

Visual Basic.Title: Type inheritance should not be recursive
Visual Basic.Description: Recursion is a technique used to define a problem in terms of the problem itself, usually in terms of a simpler version of the problem itself.

C#.Title: Optional parameters should be passed to "base" calls
C#.Description: When optional parameter values are not passed to base method calls, the value passed in by the caller is ignored. This can cause the function to behave differently than expected, leading to errors and making the code difficult to debug.

Visual Basic.Title: Optional parameters should be passed to "base" calls
Visual Basic.Description: When optional parameter values are not passed to base method calls, the value passed in by the caller is ignored. This can cause the function to behave differently than expected, leading to errors and making the code difficult to debug.

C#.Title: Empty "default" clauses should be removed
C#.Description: The default clause should take appropriate action. Having an empty default is a waste of keystrokes.

C#.Title: "ServiceContract" and "OperationContract" attributes should be used together
C#.Description: The ServiceContract attribute specifies that a class or interface defines the communication contract of a Windows Communication Foundation (WCF) service. The service operations of this class or interface are defined by OperationContract attributes added to methods. It doesn’t make sense to define a contract without any service operations; thus, in a ServiceContract class or interface at least one method should be annotated with OperationContract. Similarly, WCF only serves OperationContract methods that are defined inside ServiceContract classes or interfaces; thus, this rule also checks that ServiceContract is added to the containing type of OperationContract methods.

C#.Title: One-way "OperationContract" methods should have "void" return type
C#.Description: When declaring a Windows Communication Foundation (WCF) OperationContract method as one-way, that service method won’t return any result, not even an underlying empty confirmation message. These are fire-and-forget methods that are useful in event-like communication. Therefore, specifying a return type has no effect and can confuse readers.

Visual Basic.Title: One-way "OperationContract" methods should have "void" return type
Visual Basic.Description: When declaring a Windows Communication Foundation (WCF) OperationContract method as one-way, that service method won’t return any result, not even an underlying empty confirmation message. These are fire-and-forget methods that are useful in event-like communication. Therefore, specifying a return type has no effect and can confuse readers.

C#.Title: "params" should not be introduced on overrides
C#.Description: Adding params to a method override has no effect. The compiler accepts it, but the callers won’t be able to benefit from the added modifier.

C#.Title: Methods with "Pure" attribute should return a value
C#.Description: Marking a method with the Pure attribute indicates that the method doesn’t make any visible state changes. Therefore, a Pure method should return a result. Otherwise, it indicates a no-operation call.

Visual Basic.Title: Methods with "Pure" attribute should return a value
Visual Basic.Description: Marking a method with the Pure attribute indicates that the method doesn’t make any visible state changes. Therefore, a Pure method should return a result. Otherwise, it indicates a no-operation call.

C#.Title: Member initializer values should not be redundant
C#.Description: Fields, properties and events can be initialized either inline or in the constructor. Initializing them inline and in the constructor at the same time is redundant; the inline initialization will be overridden.

C#.Title: Nullable type comparison should not be redundant
C#.Description: Calling GetType() on a nullable value type object returns the underlying value type. Therefore, comparing the returned Type object to typeof(Nullable<SomeType>) will either throw an NullReferenceException or the result will always be true or false and can be known at compile time.

C#.Title: Jump statements should not be redundant
C#.Description: Jump statements, such as return, yield break, goto, and continue are used to change the normal flow of execution in a program. However, redundant jump statements can make code difficult to read and maintain.

C#.Title: Track use of "NotImplementedException"
C#.Description: NotImplementedException is often used to mark methods which must be implemented for the overall functionality to be complete, but which the developer wants to implement later. That’s as opposed to the NotSupportedException which is thrown by methods which are required by base classes or interfaces, but which are not appropriate to the current class.

C#.Title: Cognitive Complexity of methods should not be too high
C#.Description: This rule raises an issue when the code cognitive complexity of a function is above a certain threshold.

Visual Basic.Title: Cognitive Complexity of methods should not be too high
Visual Basic.Description: This rule raises an issue when the code cognitive complexity of a function is above a certain threshold.

Visual Basic.Title: "ByVal" should not be used
Visual Basic.Description: Since Visual Studio 2010 SP1, the ByVal parameter modifier is implicitly applied, and therefore not required anymore. Removing it from your source code will improve readability.

Visual Basic.Title: "IIf" should not be used
Visual Basic.Description: Visual Basic .NET offers a non-short-circuit conditional function, IIf(), which returns either its second or third parameter based on the expression in the first parameter. Using it is slower than using If() because each parameter is unconditionally evaluated. Further, its use can lead to runtime exceptions because IIf always evaluates all three of its arguments.

C#.Title: "SafeHandle.DangerousGetHandle" should not be called
C#.Description: The SafeHandle.DangerousGetHandle method poses significant risks and should be used carefully. This method carries the inherent danger of potentially returning an invalid handle, which can result in resource leaks and security vulnerabilities. Although it is technically possible to utilize this method without encountering issues, doing so correctly requires a high level of expertise. Therefore, it is recommended to avoid using this method altogether.

Visual Basic.Title: "SafeHandle.DangerousGetHandle" should not be called
Visual Basic.Description: The SafeHandle.DangerousGetHandle method poses significant risks and should be used carefully. This method carries the inherent danger of potentially returning an invalid handle, which can result in resource leaks and security vulnerabilities. Although it is technically possible to utilize this method without encountering issues, doing so correctly requires a high level of expertise. Therefore, it is recommended to avoid using this method altogether.

C#.Title: Exception types should be "public"
C#.Description: The point of having custom exception types is to convey more information than is available in standard types. But custom exception types must be public for that to work.

Visual Basic.Title: Exception types should be "Public"
Visual Basic.Description: The point of having custom exception types is to convey more information than is available in standard types. But custom exception types must be public for that to work.

C#.Title: Parameter names should not duplicate the names of their methods
C#.Description: The name of a method should communicate what it does, and the names of its parameters should indicate how they’re used. If a method and its parameter have the same name it is an indication that one of these rules of thumb has been broken, if not both. Even if by some trick of language that’s not the case, it is still likely to confuse callers and maintainers.

C#.Title: "out" and "ref" parameters should not be used
C#.Description: Passing a parameter by reference, which is what happens when you use the out or ref parameter modifiers, means that the method will receive a pointer to the argument, rather than the argument itself. If the argument was a value type, the method will be able to change the argument’s values. If it was a reference type, then the method receives a pointer to a pointer, which is usually not what was intended. Even when it is what was intended, this is the sort of thing that’s difficult to get right, and should be used with caution.

C#.Title: "operator==" should not be overloaded on reference types
C#.Description: The use of == to compare two objects is expected to do a reference comparison. That is, it is expected to return true if and only if they are the same object instance. Overloading the operator to do anything else will inevitably lead to the introduction of bugs by callers.

C#.Title: Strings or integral types should be used for indexers
C#.Description: Strings and integral types are typically used as indexers. When some other type is required, it typically indicates design problems, and potentially a situation where a method should be used instead.

C#.Title: Exceptions should not be thrown from unexpected methods
C#.Description: The rule is reporting when an exception is thrown from certain methods and constructors. These methods are expected to behave in a specific way and throwing an exception from them can lead to unexpected behavior and break the calling code.

C#.Title: Arrays should not be created for params parameters
C#.Description: Creating an array or using a collection expression solely for the purpose of passing it to a params parameter is unnecessary. Simply pass the elements directly, and they will be automatically consolidated into the appropriate collection type.

Visual Basic.Title: Arrays should not be created for ParamArray parameters
Visual Basic.Description: There’s no point in creating an array solely for the purpose of passing it to a ParamArray parameter. Simply pass the elements directly. They will be consolidated into an array automatically.

C#.Title: Finalizers should not be empty
C#.Description: Finalizers come with a performance cost due to the overhead of tracking the life cycle of objects. An empty one is consequently costly with no benefit or justification.

C#.Title: "IDisposable" should be implemented correctly
C#.Description: The IDisposable interface is a mechanism to release unmanaged resources, if not implemented correctly this could result in resource leaks or more severe bugs.

C#.Title: "CoSetProxyBlanket" and "CoInitializeSecurity" should not be used
C#.Description: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

Visual Basic.Title: "CoSetProxyBlanket" and "CoInitializeSecurity" should not be used
Visual Basic.Description: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

C#.Title: "Assembly.Load" should be used
C#.Description: The parameter to Assembly.Load includes the full specification of the dll to be loaded. Use another method, and you might end up with a dll other than the one you expected.

C#.Title: Mutable, non-private fields should not be "readonly"
C#.Description: Using the readonly keyword on a field means it can’t be changed after initialization. However, that’s only partly true when applied to collections or arrays. The readonly keyword enforces that another instance can’t be assigned to the field, but it cannot keep the contents from being updated. In practice, the field value can be changed, and the use of readonly on such a field is misleading, and you’re likely not getting the behavior you expect.

C#.Title: "Thread.Resume" and "Thread.Suspend" should not be used
C#.Description: Thread.Suspend and Thread.Resume can give unpredictable results, and both methods have been deprecated. Indeed, if Thread.Suspend is not used very carefully, a thread can be suspended while holding a lock, thus leading to a deadlock.

Visual Basic.Title: "Thread.Resume" and "Thread.Suspend" should not be used
Visual Basic.Description: Thread.Suspend and Thread.Resume can give unpredictable results, and both methods have been deprecated. Indeed, if Thread.Suspend is not used very carefully, a thread can be suspended while holding a lock, thus leading to a deadlock.

C#.Title: Classes that provide "Equals(<T>)" should implement "IEquatable<T>"
C#.Description: The IEquatable<T> interface has only one method in it: Equals(<T>). If you’ve already written Equals(T), there’s no reason not to explicitly implement IEquatable<T>. Doing so expands the utility of your class by allowing it to be used where an IEquatable is called for.

C#.Title: Value types should implement "IEquatable<T>"
C#.Description: If you’re using a struct, it is likely because you’re interested in performance. But by failing to implement IEquatable<T> you’re loosing performance when comparisons are made because without IEquatable<T>, boxing and reflection are used to make comparisons.

Visual Basic.Title: Value types should implement "IEquatable<T>"
Visual Basic.Description: If you’re using a Structure, it is likely because you’re interested in performance. But by failing to implement IEquatable<T> you’re loosing performance when comparisons are made because without IEquatable<T>, boxing and reflection are used to make comparisons.

C#.Title: "Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly" should not be called
C#.Description: Using Type.Assembly to get the current assembly is nearly free in terms of performance; it’s a simple property access. On the other hand, Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly() can take up to 30 times as long because it walks up the call stack to find the assembly.

C#.Title: Types should be defined in named namespaces
C#.Description: Types are declared in namespaces in order to prevent name collisions and as a way to organize them into the object hierarchy. Types that are defined outside any named namespace are in a global namespace that cannot be referenced in code.

Visual Basic.Title: Types should be defined in named namespaces
Visual Basic.Description: Types are declared in namespaces in order to prevent name collisions and as a way to organize them into the object hierarchy. Types that are defined outside any named namespace are in a global namespace that cannot be referenced in code.

C#.Title: Assemblies should have version information
C#.Description: The AssemblyVersion attribute is used to specify the version number of an assembly. An assembly is a compiled unit of code, which can be marked with a version number by applying the attribute to an assembly’s source code file.

Visual Basic.Title: Assemblies should have version information
Visual Basic.Description: The AssemblyVersion attribute is used to specify the version number of an assembly. An assembly is a compiled unit of code, which can be marked with a version number by applying the attribute to an assembly’s source code file.

C#.Title: Event Handlers should have the correct signature
C#.Description: Delegate event handlers (i.e. delegates used as type of an event) should have a very specific signature:

C#.Title: Generic event handlers should be used
C#.Description: Since .Net Framework version 2.0 it is not necessary to declare a delegate that specifies a class derived from System.EventArgs. The System.EventHandler<TEventArgs> delegate mechanism should be used instead as it allows any class derived from EventArgs to be used with that handler.

C#.Title: Collections should implement the generic interface
C#.Description: The NET Framework 2.0 introduced the generic interface System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable<T> and it should be preferred over the older, non generic, interfaces.

C#.Title: All branches in a conditional structure should not have exactly the same implementation
C#.Description: Having all branches of a switch or if chain with the same implementation indicates a problem.

Visual Basic.Title: All branches in a conditional structure should not have exactly the same implementation
Visual Basic.Description: Having all branches of a Select Case or If chain with the same implementation indicates a problem.

C#.Title: "ISerializable" should be implemented correctly
C#.Description: The ISerializable interface is the mechanism to control the type serialization process. If not implemented correctly this could result in an invalid serialization and hard-to-detect bugs.

C#.Title: Deserialization methods should be provided for "OptionalField" members
C#.Description: Fields marked with System.Runtime.Serialization.OptionalFieldAttribute are serialized just like any other field. But such fields are ignored on deserialization, and retain the default values associated with their types. Therefore, deserialization event handlers should be declared to set such fields during the deserialization process.

Visual Basic.Title: Deserialization methods should be provided for "OptionalField" members
Visual Basic.Description: Fields marked with System.Runtime.Serialization.OptionalFieldAttribute are serialized just like any other field. But such fields are ignored on deserialization, and retain the default values associated with their types. Therefore, deserialization event handlers should be declared to set such fields during the deserialization process.

C#.Title: Serialization event handlers should be implemented correctly
C#.Description: Serialization event handlers that don’t have the correct signature will not be called, bypassing augmentations to automated serialization and deserialization events.

Visual Basic.Title: Serialization event handlers should be implemented correctly
Visual Basic.Description: Serialization event handlers that don’t have the correct signature will not be called, bypassing augmentations to automated serialization and deserialization events.

C#.Title: Parameter names used into ArgumentException constructors should match an existing one
C#.Description: Some constructors of the ArgumentException, ArgumentNullException, ArgumentOutOfRangeException and DuplicateWaitObjectException classes must be fed with a valid parameter name. This rule raises an issue in two cases:

C#.Title: Number patterns should be regular
C#.Description: The use of punctuation characters to separate subgroups in a number can make the number more readable. For instance consider 1,000,000,000 versus 1000000000. But when the grouping is irregular, such as 1,000,00,000; it indicates an error.

C#.Title: "Generic.List" instances should not be part of public APIs
C#.Description: System.Collections.Generic.List<T> is a generic collection that is designed for performance and not inheritance. For example, it does not contain virtual members that make it easier to change the behavior of an inherited class. That means that future attempts to expand the behavior will be spoiled because the extension points simply aren’t there. Instead, one of the following generic collections should be used:

C#.Title: "static readonly" constants should be "const" instead
C#.Description: The value of a static readonly field is computed at runtime while the value of a const field is calculated at compile time, which improves performance.

C#.Title: "static" fields should be initialized inline
C#.Description: When a static constructor serves no other purpose that initializing static fields, it comes with an unnecessary performance cost because the compiler generates a check before each static method or instance constructor invocation.

C#.Title: Multidimensional arrays should not be used
C#.Description: A jagged array is an array whose elements are arrays. It is recommended over a multidimensional array because the arrays that make up the elements can be of different sizes, which avoids wasting memory space.

C#.Title: "GC.SuppressFinalize" should not be called
C#.Description: GC.SuppressFinalize requests that the system not call the finalizer for the specified object. This should only be done when implementing Dispose as part of the Dispose Pattern.

C#.Title: Conditionals should start on new lines
C#.Description: Placing an if statement on the same line as the closing } from a preceding if, else, or else if block can lead to confusion and potential errors. It may indicate a missing else statement or create ambiguity for maintainers who might fail to understand that the two statements are unconnected.

C#.Title: A conditionally executed single line should be denoted by indentation
C#.Description: When the line immediately after conditional statements has neither curly braces nor indentation, the intent of the code is unclear and perhaps not executed as expected. Additionally, such code is confusing to maintainers.

C#.Title: Collection sizes and array length comparisons should make sense
C#.Description: The size of a collection and the length of an array are always greater than or equal to zero. Testing it doesn’t make sense, since the result is always true.

C#.Description: Creating a new Exception without actually throwing does not achieve the intended purpose.

C#.Description: String representations of URIs or URLs are prone to parsing and encoding errors which can lead to vulnerabilities. The System.Uri class is a safe alternative and should be preferred.

C#.Description: Objects that can be accessed across application domain boundaries are said to have weak identity. This means that these objects can be considered shared resources outside of the domain, which can be lead to them being accessed or modified by multiple threads or concurrent parts of a program, outside of the domain.

C#.Title: Pointers to unmanaged memory should not be visible
C#.Description: Pointer and unmanaged function pointer types such as IntPtr, UIntPtr, int* etc. are used to access unmanaged memory, usually in order to use C or C++ libraries. If such a pointer is not secured by making it private, internal or readonly, it can lead to a vulnerability allowing access to arbitrary locations.

C#.Title: Collection properties should be readonly
C#.Description: A writable collection property can be replaced by a completely different collection. Making it readonly prevents that while still allowing individual members to be set. If you want to allow the replacement of the whole collection the recommended pattern is to implement a method to remove all the elements (e.g. System.Collections.List<T>.Clear) and a method to populate the collection (e.g. System.Collections.List<T>.AddRange).

C#.Title: "System.Uri" arguments should be used instead of strings
C#.Description: String representations of URIs or URLs are prone to parsing and encoding errors which can lead to vulnerabilities. The System.Uri class is a safe alternative and should be preferred.

C#.Title: Inherited member visibility should not be decreased
C#.Description: Decreasing the accessibility level of an inherited method that is not overridable to private will shadow the name of the base method and can lead to confusion.

C#.Title: Enumeration members should not be named "Reserved"
C#.Description: If an enum member’s name contains the word "reserved" it implies it is not currently used and will be change in the future. However changing an enum member is a breaking change and can create significant problems. There is no need to reserve an enum member since a new member can be added in the future, and such an addition will usually not be a breaking change.

C#.Title: Method signatures should not contain nested generic types
C#.Description: A nested type is a type argument that is also a generic type. Calling a method with such a nested type argument requires complicated and confusing code. It should be avoided as much as possible.

C#.Title: All type parameters should be used in the parameter list to enable type inference
C#.Description: Type inference enables the call of a generic method without explicitly specifying its type arguments. This is not possible when a parameter type is missing from the argument list.

C#.Title: Enumerations should have "Int32" storage
C#.Description: By default the storage type of an enum is Int32. In most cases it is not necessary to change this. In particular you will not achieve any performance gain by using a smaller data type (e.g. Byte) and may limit future uses.

C#.Title: Interfaces should not be empty
C#.Description: Empty interfaces should be avoided as they do not provide any functional requirements for implementing classes.

C#.Title: Child class fields should not differ from parent class fields only by capitalization
C#.Description: Having a field in a child class with a name that differs from a parent class' field only by capitalization is sure to cause confusion. Such child class fields should be renamed.

C#.Title: Assemblies should be marked with "NeutralResourcesLanguageAttribute"
C#.Description: It is important to inform the ResourceManager of the language used to display the resources of the neutral culture for an assembly. This improves lookup performance for the first resource loaded.

C#.Title: Classes implementing "IEquatable<T>" should be sealed
C#.Description: When a class implements the IEquatable<T> interface, it enters a contract that, in effect, states "I know how to compare two instances of type T or any type derived from T for equality.". However if that class is derived, it is very unlikely that the base class will know how to make a meaningful comparison. Therefore that implicit contract is now broken.

C#.Title: Searching OS commands in PATH is security-sensitive
C#.Description: When you run an OS command, it is always important to protect yourself against the risk of accidental or malicious replacement of the executables in the production system.

Visual Basic.Title: Searching OS commands in PATH is security-sensitive
Visual Basic.Description: When you run an OS command, it is always important to protect yourself against the risk of accidental or malicious replacement of the executables in the production system.

C#.Title: Interface methods should be callable by derived types
C#.Description: When a base type explicitly implements a public interface method, property or event, that member is only accessible in derived types through a reference to the current instance (namely this). If the derived type explicitly overrides that interface member, the base implementation becomes inaccessible.

C#.Title: Strings should be normalized to uppercase
C#.Description: Certain characters, once normalized to lowercase, cannot make a round trip. That is, they can not be converted from one locale to another and then accurately restored to their original characters.

C#.Title: Type names should not match namespaces
C#.Description: When a type name matches the name of a publicly defined namespace, for instance one in the .NET framework class library, it leads to confusion and makes the library that much harder to use.

C#.Title: Generics should be used when appropriate
C#.Description: When a reference parameter (keyword ref) is used, the passed argument type must exactly match the reference parameter type. This means that to be able to pass a derived type, it must be cast and assigned to a variable of the proper type. Use of generic methods eliminates that cumbersome down casting and should therefore be preferred.

C#.Title: Properties should be preferred
C#.Description: Properties are accessed like fields which makes them easier to use.

C#.Title: Operators should be overloaded consistently
C#.Description: When overloading some arithmetic operator overloads, it is very important to make sure that all related operators and methods are consistent in their implementation.

C#.Title: Types should not extend outdated base types
C#.Description: With the advent of .NET Framework 2.0, certain practices and types have become obsolete.

C#.Title: Literals should not be passed as localized parameters
C#.Description: String literals embedded in the source code will not be localized properly.

C#.Title: Overloads with a "CultureInfo" or an "IFormatProvider" parameter should be used
C#.Description: When a System.Globalization.CultureInfo or IFormatProvider object is not supplied, the default value that is supplied by the overloaded member might not have the effect that you want in all locales.

C#.Title: Locales should be set for data types
C#.Description: When you create a DataTable or DataSet, you should set the locale explicitly. By default, the locale for these types is the current culture. For data that is stored in a database or file and is shared globally, the locale should ordinarily be set to the invariant culture (CultureInfo.InvariantCulture).

C#.Title: Overloads with a "StringComparison" parameter should be used
C#.Description: Many string operations, the Compare and Equals methods in particular, provide an overload that accepts a StringComparison enumeration value as a parameter. Calling these overloads and explicitly providing this parameter makes your code clearer and easier to maintain.

C#.Title: Property names should not match get methods
C#.Description: Properties and Get method should have names that makes them clearly distinguishable.

C#.Title: Non-abstract attributes should be sealed
C#.Description: The .NET framework class library provides methods for retrieving custom attributes. Sealing the attribute eliminates the search through the inheritance hierarchy, and can improve performance.

Visual Basic.Title: Non-abstract attributes should be sealed
Visual Basic.Description: The .NET framework class library provides methods for retrieving custom attributes. Sealing the attribute eliminates the search through the inheritance hierarchy, and can improve performance.

C#.Title: "params" should be used instead of "varargs"
C#.Description: A method using the VarArgs calling convention is not Common Language Specification (CLS) compliant and might not be accessible across programming languages, while the params keyword works the same way and is CLS compliant.

C#.Title: Non-flags enums should not be marked with "FlagsAttribute"
C#.Description: This rule raises an issue when an externally visible enumeration is marked with FlagsAttribute and one, or more, of its values is not a power of 2 or a combination of the other defined values.

C#.Title: Method overloads should be grouped together
C#.Description: For clarity, all overloads of the same method should be grouped together. That lets both users and maintainers quickly understand all the current available options.

Visual Basic.Title: Method overloads should be grouped together
Visual Basic.Description: For clarity, all overloads of the same method should be grouped together. That lets both users and maintainers quickly understand all the current available options.

C#.Title: Collection elements should not be replaced unconditionally
C#.Description: Storing a value inside a collection at a given key or index and then unconditionally overwriting it without reading the initial value is a case of a "dead store".

Visual Basic.Title: Map values should not be replaced unconditionally

C#.Title: Methods should not have identical implementations
C#.Description: Two methods having the same implementation are suspicious. It might be that something else was intended. Or the duplication is intentional, which becomes a maintenance burden.

C#.Description: The Attributed Programming Model, also known as Attribute-oriented programming (@OP), is a programming model used to embed attributes within codes.

C#.Title: Native methods should be wrapped
C#.Description: Native methods are functions that reside in libraries outside the .NET runtime. Calling them is helpful for interoperability with applications and libraries written in other programming languages, mainly when performing platform-specific operations. However, doing so comes with additional risks since it means stepping out of the memory-safety model of the runtime. It is therefore highly recommended to take extra steps, like input validation, when invoking native methods. Making the native method private and providing a wrapper that performs these additional steps is the best way to do so.

C#.Title: Null checks should not be combined with "is" operator checks
C#.Description: There’s no need to null test in conjunction with an is test. null is not an instance of anything, so a null check is redundant.

Visual Basic.Title: Null checks should not be combined with "TypeOf Is" operator checks
Visual Basic.Description: There’s no need to null test in conjunction with an TypeOf ... Is test. Nothing is not an instance of anything, so a null check is redundant.

C#.Title: Windows Forms entry points should be marked with STAThread
C#.Description: When an assembly uses Windows Forms (classes and interfaces from the System.Windows.Forms namespace) its entry point should be marked with the STAThreadAttribute to indicate that the threading model should be "Single-Threaded Apartment" (STA) which is the only one supported by Windows Forms.

C#.Title: Members should not have conflicting transparency annotations
C#.Description: Transparency attributes in the .NET Framework, designed to protect security-critical operations, can lead to ambiguities and vulnerabilities when declared at different levels such as both for the class and a method.

C#.Title: Extension methods should not extend "object"
C#.Description: ﻿Creating an extension method that extends object is not recommended because it makes the method available on every type. Extensions should be applied at the most specialized level possible, and that is very unlikely to be object.

C#.Title: Extensions should be in separate namespaces
C#.Description: It makes little sense to create an extension method when it is possible to just add that method to the class itself.

C#.Description: When creating a custom Markup Extension that accepts parameters in WPF, the ConstructorArgument markup must be used to identify the discrete properties that match these parameters. C#.Title: Methods should be named according to their synchronicities
C#.Description: According to the Task-based Asynchronous Pattern (TAP), methods returning either a System.Threading.Tasks.Task or a System.Threading.Tasks.Task<TResult> are considered "asynchronous". Such methods should use the Async suffix. Conversely methods which do not return such Tasks should not have an "Async" suffix in their names.

C#.Title: Getters and setters should access the expected fields
C#.Description: Properties provide a way to enforce encapsulation by providing accessors that give controlled access to private fields. However, in classes with multiple fields, it is not unusual that copy-and-paste is used to quickly create the needed properties, which can result in the wrong field being accessed by a getter or setter.

C#.Title: "Shared" parts should not be created with "new"
C#.Description: Marking a class with PartCreationPolicy(CreationPolicy.Shared), which is part of Managed Extensibility Framework (MEF), means that a single, shared instance of the exported object will be created. Therefore it doesn’t make sense to create new instances using the constructor and it will most likely result in unexpected behaviours.

C#.Title: Parameter validation in yielding methods should be wrapped
C#.Description: Because of the way yield methods are rewritten by the compiler (they become lazily evaluated state machines) any exceptions thrown during the parameters check will happen only when the collection is iterated over. That could happen far away from the source of the buggy code.

C#.Title: Parameter validation in "async"/"await" methods should be wrapped
C#.Description: Because of the way async/await methods are rewritten by the compiler, any exceptions thrown during the parameters check will happen only when the task is observed. That could happen far away from the source of the buggy code or never happen for fire-and-forget tasks.

C#.Title: Calls to "async" methods should not be blocking
C#.Description: Making blocking calls to async methods transforms code that was intended to be asynchronous into a blocking operation. Doing so can cause deadlocks and unexpected blocking of context threads.

C#.Title: Unread "private" fields should be removed
C#.Description: Private fields which are written but never read are a case of "dead store". Changing the value of such a field is useless and most probably indicates an error in the code.

C#.Title: Disabling CSRF protections is security-sensitive
C#.Description: A cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attack occurs when a trusted user of a web application can be forced, by an attacker, to perform sensitive actions that he didn’t intend, such as updating his profile or sending a message, more generally anything that can change the state of the application.

C#.Title: Delivering code in production with debug features activated is security-sensitive
C#.Description: Development tools and frameworks usually have options to make debugging easier for developers. Although these features are useful during development, they should never be enabled for applications deployed in production. Debug instructions or error messages can leak detailed information about the system, like the application’s path or file names.

C#.Title: Expanding archive files without controlling resource consumption is security-sensitive
C#.Description: Successful Zip Bomb attacks occur when an application expands untrusted archive files without controlling the size of the expanded data, which can lead to denial of service. A Zip bomb is usually a malicious archive file of a few kilobytes of compressed data but turned into gigabytes of uncompressed data. To achieve this extreme compression ratio, attackers will compress irrelevant data (eg: a long string of repeated bytes).

C#.Title: Using clear-text protocols is security-sensitive
C#.Description: Clear-text protocols such as ftp, telnet, or http lack encryption of transported data, as well as the capability to build an authenticated connection. It means that an attacker able to sniff traffic from the network can read, modify, or corrupt the transported content. C#.Title: Passwords should not be stored in plaintext or with a fast hashing algorithm
C#.Description: The improper storage of passwords poses a significant security risk to software applications. This vulnerability arises when passwords are stored in plaintext or with a fast hashing algorithm. To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker typically requires access to the stored passwords.

C#.Title: Using publicly writable directories is security-sensitive
C#.Description: Operating systems have global directories where any user has write access. Those folders are mostly used as temporary storage areas like /tmp in Linux based systems. An application manipulating files from these folders is exposed to race conditions on filenames: a malicious user can try to create a file with a predictable name before the application does. A successful attack can result in other files being accessed, modified, corrupted or deleted. This risk is even higher if the application runs with elevated permissions.

C#.Title: Insecure temporary file creation methods should not be used
C#.Description: Temporary files are considered insecurely created when the file existence check is performed separately from the actual file creation. Such a situation can occur when creating temporary files using normal file handling functions or when using dedicated temporary file handling functions that are not atomic.

This will likely lead to confusion and potential bugs.
